The question of whether GMOs should be part of our diet is marked by genuinely conflicting opinions and research outcomes. Major health organizations, including the American Medical Association and the World Health Organization, have concluded from independent research worldwide that genetically modified foods are safe for consumers [d1], a position echoed by the FDA, EPA, and USDA [d2], Health Canada [d5], and a 2016 National Academy of Sciences report involving 50 scientists [d6]. Numerous studies have shown no health risks associated with GMO/BE food consumption, and bioengineering can even improve nutritional content and reduce harmful agricultural chemical residues [d4]. However, opposing voices persist: anti-GMO advocacy groups such as the Institute for Responsible Technology have claimed that all GMOs carry high toxicity risk, and some researchers in 2009 suggested GMO foods might negatively impact the liver, kidney, pancreas, and reproductive system, though they lacked evidence to confirm this and called for further studies [d1][d3]. Public skepticism remains substantial — a 2018 IFIC survey found that 47% of respondents avoid GMO foods at least somewhat, even as the scientific community broadly affirms their safety [d6].
